name: lightning
desc: Generates assembly language code at run-time
why: GNU JIT library generating machine code at runtime; a door into how compilers and JITs actually emit assembly.

brief.what_it_is: GNU lightning is a library that generates assembly language code at run-time. It exposes a standardized RISC instruction set, loosely inspired by MIPS and SPARC, so client code is written once against that set and the library emits machine code for the target CPU. The homepage lists backends for aarch64, alpha, arm, hppa, ia64, loongarch, mips, powerpc, risc-v, s390, sparc and x86. The page does not describe the exact inputs and outputs of the API beyond this.
brief.why_it_exists: The page says the library is very fast, which makes it ideal for Just-In-Time compilers, and that it abstracts over the target CPU so clients do not have to write per-architecture code generators.
brief.how_it_works: Clients emit instructions in lightning's standardized RISC-style instruction set at run-time, and the library translates them into native code for the architecture it was built for, using per-architecture backends. The homepage does not go into further detail on the mechanism.
brief.install_notes: The homepage gives no build or install steps. It says releases are available from ftp.gnu.org, documentation is available online (no link given in the page text), and the Git repository is at git.savannah.gnu.org. Contact is Paulo Andrade, with a mailing list for bug reports and more information. The brew entry lists no executables, so this is a library, not a command-line tool.
brief.standout: It is a code generation library rather than a compiler: it targets a fixed RISC-style instruction set and leaves the rest to the caller, which makes it a small, readable window into how JITs emit machine code across many CPU families. The backend list is unusually long for a project of this size.
brief.status: Unknown as to release cadence. The homepage copyright runs 2014-2023 and the page footer shows an update date of 2026/01/06, which reflects the web page, not a software release. No release version, last commit date or README was read, so the project's activity level could not be confirmed from this page.
brief.caveats: The homepage is a thin project page with no README, examples or commands, and its documentation and repository links are described but not given as URLs in the text. The page says the library is 'usable in complex code generation tasks' but does not give a maturity level or list known limitations. The page is licensed CC BY-ND 3.0 US; the software's own license was not stated on this page.

judge.reason: Its portable RISC-like instruction set turns runtime code generation into a compact way to explore how JITs emit native machine code across many architectures.

entry.title: GNU lightning
entry.tldr: A GNU library that emits native machine code at run-time from one RISC-style instruction set, so a JIT does not need a code generator per CPU.
entry.deeper_look:
GNU lightning is a library, not a command. A program calls it to write instructions into memory while running, and the library turns them into native code for the CPU it was built for. The caller writes against one standardized RISC instruction set, which the homepage says is "inspired by the MIPS and SPARC chips."

The reason for it, per the project page, is speed and portability. The library is described as "very fast, making it ideal for Just-In-Time compilers," and it spares clients from writing a separate code generator for each architecture. The homepage lists backends for aarch64, alpha, arm, hppa, ia64, loongarch, mips, powerpc, risc-v, s390, sparc and x86.

The idea underneath is how a JIT actually works: choose a simple intermediate instruction set, then map it onto each real processor. Lightning is a code generation layer rather than a compiler, so the rest is left to the caller. That makes it a small way to see how machine code gets emitted across many CPU families.

The homepage is thin. It gives no API details, examples or commands, so expect to read the documentation and source to learn how it is used.
entry.install:
brew install lightning
# This installs a library only: no executables. You will need a C compiler and your own program to call it. The homepage gives no build steps; releases are on ftp.gnu.org and the source is on git.savannah.gnu.org.
entry.whats_unique: It is a plain code generation library with a fixed RISC-style instruction set, and the caller handles everything else. Its backend list is long for a project this small.
entry.caveats: The homepage has no README, examples or commands, and its activity level could not be confirmed, so you will be reading docs and source to get started.
